title: The keys, 1921
hookLine: the Sikhs won back the keys of the Golden Temple treasury by peaceful protest

cards: A bunch of keys on a ring. They open the toshakhana, the treasury of the Golden Temple, where its precious gifts and offerings are kept.
In late 1921, just as the new Sikh committee asks for them, an official acting for the British government takes them into the government's hands. On paper it's a small administrative step.
To Sikhs, it's a message: you may pray here, but we still hold the keys. What happens next turns a bunch of keys into a national story.

teach.b: The SGPC had begun to manage the Golden Temple. Taking the treasury keys into government hands said the British, not the Sangat, still had the last word.

Sikhs answered with meetings, speeches and refusals, all peaceful. Leaders were arrested, including Baba Kharak Singh, a respected head of the committee. More volunteers stepped forward and were arrested in their turn.
The protest spread, and the arrests didn't stop it. In the end the government backed down.

The prisoners were released, and the keys were handed to Baba Kharak Singh. Accounts say Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram of congratulation, calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won.
In a salok at Ang 1237 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru is called the key: the mind is a locked room, and only the Guru's key opens it.

That verse is about the inner life, not a treasury. But it points at what Sikhs remember about this protest: in their telling, the keys in the government's keeping were never the real power; the Sangat's discipline was.
Without striking anyone, the community won back what was theirs, and more battles were coming.

how: Sikhs remember the keys affair, the Chabian da Morcha, as an early victory of the gurdwara reform movement, won by peaceful protest; the toshakhana of the Golden Temple is still kept under the SGPC's management.

o: the temple treasury's keys, won back by peaceful protest
the gates of the Golden Temple, shut to reformers
the SGPC's seal, given to it by the government

games.q: the keys affair — tap the pairs.
p: took the keys as the committee asked

s: the Sikhs took the keys back by force
they protested peacefully; leaders and volunteers were arrested, and the government backed down.
the keys were handed to Baba Kharak Singh
the salok at Ang 1237 is about the temple treasury
it's about the inner life: the mind is a locked room, and the Guru is the key.

games.q: the government has taken the keys of the Golden Temple's treasury. your leaders are being arrested. what do the Sikhs do?
o: keep protesting peacefully, with more volunteers stepping forward.
give up and let the government keep them.
games.why: the protest stayed peaceful and kept growing; the government released the prisoners and handed the keys to Baba Kharak Singh.

practice: If there's a key nearby, hold it in your palm and feel its weight; if not, picture one.

Think of something you're working toward that won't come quickly, a change at work, a repair in a family, a habit you're breaking, and on the breath out, quietly resolve to keep going without forcing it and without giving up.
If you pray, add Waheguru to that breath.

wordCard.voice: The keys. The keys of the Golden Temple treasury, taken into government hands and won back by the Sikhs through peaceful protest. Today's word.

orig.note: kunji, key; in Gurbani the Guru is the key to the locked mind.

carryVoice: Your line: first battle won. The keys came back without a blow. Day nine hundred eighty-six, done.
